v: Jesus answered and spoke to them again in parables, saying,
“The Kingdom of Heaven is like a certain king, who made a wedding feast for his son,
and sent out his servants to call those who were invited to the wedding feast, but they would not come.

Again he sent out other servants, saying, ‘Tell those who are invited, “Behold, I have prepared my dinner. My cattle and my fatlings are killed, and all things are ready. Come to the wedding feast!” ’
But they made light of it, and went their ways, one to his own farm, another to his merchandise,
and the rest grabbed his servants, and treated them shamefully, and killed them.
When the king heard that, he was angry, and sent his armies, destroyed those murderers, and burned their city.
“Then he said to his servants, ‘The wedding is ready, but those who were invited weren’t worthy.
Go therefore to the intersections of the highways, and as many as you may find, invite to the wedding feast.’
Those servants went out into the highways, and gathered together as many as they found, both bad and good. The wedding was filled with guests.
But when the king came in to see the guests, he saw there a man who didn’t have on wedding clothing,
and he said to him, ‘Friend, how did you come in here not wearing wedding clothing?’ He was speechless.
Then the king said to the servants, ‘Bind him hand and foot, take him away, and throw him into the outer darkness. That is where the weeping and grinding of teeth will be.’
For many are called, but few chosen.”
b: In this passage Jesus uses the parable of a king giving a wedding feast for his son to reveal the truth of the Kingdom of Heaven and God's call on our lives. The parable shows God's generous invitation and the different ways people respond. The king represents God, and the wedding feast is the banquet of salvation He has prepared for us. Although the king sent out his invitation again and again, many of those invited refused to come for one reason or another, and some even treated the king's servants violently.

When all those first invited refused to attend, the king commanded his servants to go out to the highways and byways and bring in everyone they found, both bad and good. This shows that God's grace is open to all, regardless of race, status, or past conduct. Yet the parable also tells of a guest who was cast out because he had no wedding garment. This stresses that responding to God's call means more than accepting the invitation; we must respond with the right attitude and preparation.

The heart of Jesus' message is that God's salvation is proclaimed widely to everyone, but those who receive His grace must come with the right heart: reverence and gratitude toward God. This was a rebuke to the religious leaders of that day, and also a reminder to every listener that each person's response to God's grace must be sincere and prepared.
q: Consider how you have responded to God's invitation. Are you ready to receive His grace and honor Him with a fitting way of life? What changes in your life would help you prepare better for God's spiritual banquet?
pr: Dear heavenly Father, thank You for reminding us, through the parable of Jesus Christ, of Your generous invitation to us. Help us to respond to Your call with the right heart, and to prepare in humility and obedience to take part in the spiritual feast You have prepared for us. As we face the challenges and decisions of daily life, give us wisdom and courage to live out Your will and bring glory to You. In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: Then the Pharisees went and took counsel how they might entrap him in his talk.

They sent their disciples to him, along with the Herodians, saying, “Teacher, we know that you are honest, and teach the way of God in truth, no matter whom you teach, for you aren’t partial to anyone.
Tell us therefore, what do you think? Is it lawful to pay taxes to Caesar, or not?”
But Jesus perceived their wickedness, and said, “Why do you test me, you hypocrites?
Show me the tax money.” They brought to him a denarius.
He asked them, “Whose is this image and inscription?”
They said to him, “Caesar’s.” Then he said to them, “Give therefore to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s.”
When they heard it, they marveled, and left him, and went away.
b: This passage describes the Pharisees and the Herodians trying to trap Jesus with a political question: should taxes be paid to the Roman emperor? It was an obvious setup. If Jesus answered, "Do not pay," they could accuse Him of opposing Rome; if He answered, "Pay," He would lose the support of the people. Jesus' reply showed His wisdom and His faithfulness to the truth. He asked to see the coin, pointed out that the image on it was Caesar's, and then spoke the famous words: "Give to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's."

These words not only skillfully avoided a political trap but also give deep insight into faith and civic responsibility. Jesus acknowledged the legitimacy of earthly authority, yet He emphasized the supremacy of God's authority. His answer reminds us that while we fulfill our duties on earth, it is even more important to obey the principles of heaven.

Through this passage God reminds us that when we face moral and ethical choices, we should discern wisely and remain faithful. God gives us wisdom so that in every situation we can make choices that honor Him.
q: How do you practice the teaching "Give to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's" in your daily life? In your work, family, or community, where do you need to balance earthly and spiritual responsibilities more wisely?
pr: Dear heavenly Father, thank You for teaching us through Jesus Christ the balance we should keep between our earthly and spiritual responsibilities. Grant us wisdom to discern, so that in every circumstance we may represent You well, and while keeping the laws of the land, never forget the principles of heaven. In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: On that day Sadducees (those who say that there is no resurrection) came to him. They asked him,
saying, “Teacher, Moses said, ‘If a man dies, having no children, his brother shall marry his wife, and raise up offspring for his brother.’
Now there were with us seven brothers. The first married and died, and having no offspring left his wife to his brother.
In the same way, the second also, and the third, to the seventh.
After them all, the woman died.
In the resurrection therefore, whose wife will she be of the seven? For they all had her.”
But Jesus answered them, “You are mistaken, not knowing the Scriptures, nor the power of God.
For in the resurrection they neither marry, nor are given in marriage, but are like God’s angels in heaven.
But concerning the resurrection of the dead, haven’t you read that which was spoken to you by God, saying,
‘I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob?’ God is not the God of the dead, but of the living.”
When the multitudes heard it, they were astonished at his teaching.
b: In this passage, the conversation between Jesus and the Sadducees reveals the truth of the resurrection and the power of God. The Sadducees were a religious party of that time who did not believe in the resurrection. They tested Jesus with an elaborate hypothetical question, asking whose husband a woman widowed many times would be at the resurrection. Their aim was to make Jesus' teaching look absurd and so challenge what He taught about the resurrection.

Jesus' answer went straight to their error: they understood neither the Scriptures nor the power of God. He explained that in the life of the resurrection the social structure of marriage no longer applies; people will be like angels, beyond the way of life in the present world. Jesus also quoted what God said to Moses in Exodus to stress that God is the God of the living, not of the dead. Though Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob died, they are still alive in God's Kingdom, and one day their bodies will be raised too. This underlines the reality and certainty of resurrection and eternal life.

Jesus' teaching challenged the narrow thinking of the Sadducees and revealed a deeper spiritual truth: God's Kingdom is not bound by the conditions of this world, but is open to all who believe in Him.
q: In your life of faith, in which areas do you need to trust God's power more deeply? How do you see the influence of the teaching about eternal life and the resurrection on your daily life?
pr: Dear heavenly Father, we thank You for revealing to us, through Your Son Jesus Christ, the deep truths of the resurrection and eternal life. Help us to understand the Scriptures more deeply and to experience Your power in our faith. When we face questions and challenges in life, strengthen our trust and let us be sure that with You all things are possible. In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: But the Pharisees, when they heard that he had silenced the Sadducees, gathered themselves together.
One of them, a lawyer, asked him a question, testing him.
“Teacher, which is the greatest commandment in the law?”
Jesus said to him, “ ‘You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your mind.’
This is the first and great commandment.
A second likewise is this, ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself.’
The whole law and the prophets depend on these two commandments.”
b: In this passage Jesus answers a question from a lawyer who was testing Him. He asked, "Teacher, which is the greatest commandment in the law?" This was a key question, because the Jewish law contained many commandments, and knowing which one was most basic was vital for putting faith into practice.

Jesus' answer was clear and profound: "You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your mind." This is the greatest commandment and the foundation of all the others. Jesus went on to give the second: "You shall love your neighbor as yourself." It is bound up with the first, because one true expression of loving God is loving those He has made, our neighbors, since people are made in the image and likeness of God. Jesus concluded that on these two commandments "the whole law and the prophets depend." This means that all the teaching of the law and the prophets aims to guide us in learning how to love God and love others.

This passage shows us that the heart of the Christian faith is relationship: our relationship with God and our relationship with others. By summing up the whole law and the prophets in these two commandments, Jesus reminds us that however many religious rituals or rules we keep, they are empty if we fail to express sincere love.
q: How do you practice the two commandments to love God and to love your neighbor as yourself in your daily life? What concrete actions could help you live them out more deeply?
pr: Dear heavenly Father, thank You for teaching us through Your Son Jesus Christ that love is the foundation of fulfilling Your law. Help us love You and our neighbors more each day, and let this love become the expression of our lives. Guide us to show the love of Christ in every interaction, so that our lives may be a testimony to Your love. In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: Now while the Pharisees were gathered together, Jesus asked them a question,
saying, “What do you think of the Christ? Whose son is he?” They said to him, “Of David.”
He said to them, “How then does David in the Spirit call him Lord, saying,
‘The Lord said to my Lord, sit on my right hand, until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet?’
“If then David calls him Lord, how is he his son?”
No one was able to answer him a word, neither did any man dare ask him any more questions from that day forward.
b: In this passage Jesus puts a question about the Messiah to the Pharisees gathered around Him, challenging their understanding of who the Messiah is. He asked them, "What do you think of the Christ? Whose son is he?" The Pharisees answered, "Of David." This answer was commonly accepted among the Jews at that time, because the Messiah had been prophesied as a descendant of King David, a political and spiritual savior who was to come.

Jesus then quoted David's own words (Psalm 110) and asked, "If then David calls him Lord, how is he his son?" Here Jesus pointed to a profound spiritual truth: even though the Christ descends from David by blood, His identity and position far surpass David's, since even David called Him Lord. This points to Jesus being not only the Son of Man but also the Son of God, whose authority is above all, even above His ancestor David.

Jesus' question reveals His deity and a deeper revelation of the Messiah's identity. It also shows that although the Pharisees knew the Scriptures well, they did not grasp their deeper spiritual meaning. The conversation ended with no one able to answer Jesus, and from that day on no one dared to question Him publicly.

The importance of this question is that it challenges our understanding of God and His Messiah: God is not only a figure in history but the eternal Lord, and His Kingdom and authority far exceed our usual understanding.
q: How do you understand Jesus' dual identity as both David's descendant and David's Lord? What does this mean for your life of faith?
pr: Dear heavenly Father, thank You for revealing the deity and authority of Jesus Christ through Your Word. Help us to understand Your nature and Your will more deeply, so that we may know more fully who Jesus is and live out our faith in You. When we face the various challenges of life, give us wisdom and confidence to follow You steadfastly. In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: Then Jesus spoke to the multitudes and to his disciples,
saying, “The scribes and the Pharisees sat on Moses’ seat.
All things therefore whatever they tell you to observe, observe and do, but don’t do their works; for they say, and don’t do.
For they bind heavy burdens that are grievous to be borne, and lay them on men’s shoulders; but they themselves will not lift a finger to help them.
But they do all their works to be seen by men. They make their phylacteries  broad, enlarge the fringes of their garments,
and love the place of honor at feasts, the best seats in the synagogues,
the salutations in the marketplaces, and to be called ‘Rabbi, Rabbi’ by men.
But don’t you be called ‘Rabbi,’ for one is your teacher, the Christ, and all of you are brothers.
Call no man on the earth your father, for one is your Father, he who is in heaven.
Neither be called masters, for one is your master, the Christ.
But he who is greatest among you will be your servant.
Whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted.
b: In this passage Jesus sharply criticizes the hypocrisy of the scribes and the Pharisees. Although they sat in Moses' seat and had authority to teach the law, their conduct did not match what they taught. Jesus pointed out that while they told others to keep the law, they did not practice it themselves, and their deeds were done only to win the praise and respect of others.

Jesus went on to reveal the attitude a true spiritual leader should have: humility and service. He taught His disciples not to seek to be called "Rabbi," nor to seek high positions in society or any other form of honor, because in God's Kingdom true greatness comes from serving others. Leadership in God's Kingdom is completely different from worldly leadership; it should rest on humility and service.

This passage shows us the true meaning of spiritual authority: not control or oppression, but reflecting the love and authority of Christ through humility and service. Jesus Himself is that example. He taught not only with words but by His own life, and in the end He gave Himself on the cross to bring redemption to all of us.
q: In what areas of your life might you be seeking worldly honor rather than serving? How do you practice the humility and service Jesus taught in your daily life?
pr: Dear heavenly Father, thank You for showing us, through Your Son Jesus Christ, what true spiritual leadership should be. Help us learn Jesus' humility and service, not seeking worldly glory but seeking to serve and to love our neighbors as ourselves. In our daily lives, make us more like Christ, and let us be a light of Your love and truth. In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you devour widows’ houses, and as a pretense you make long prayers. Therefore you will receive greater condemnation.
“But woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! Because you shut up the Kingdom of Heaven against men; for you don’t enter in yourselves, neither do you allow those who are entering in to enter.
Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you travel around by sea and land to make one proselyte; and when he becomes one, you make him twice as much a son of Gehenna as yourselves.
b: In this passage Jesus continues His severe rebuke of the scribes and the Pharisees. They are accused of hypocrisy and of spiritual oppression. Jesus charged them with shutting the door of the Kingdom of Heaven in people's faces, neither entering themselves nor allowing others to enter. This underlines the responsibility of religious leaders: they ought to be examples who lead people near to God, not obstacles.

Jesus' words reveal that the conduct of the scribes and Pharisees was extremely selfish and manipulative. On the surface they kept the law, but in reality they neglected its spirit, love for God and love for others. Such conduct leads to spiritual death rather than the fullness of life.

Jesus also condemns their zeal in making converts, pointing out that even when they worked hard at it, their motives were wrong, and they led people into even deeper lostness rather than true salvation. This shows how important the motive behind our actions is, and warns believers to beware of leaders who do injustice in the name of righteousness.
This series of rebukes from Jesus calls us to reflect deeply on our own practice of faith: do we also sometimes follow our faith outwardly while in reality neglecting what it truly requires?
q: In your practice of faith, in what areas might there be hypocrisy? How can you be more honest about your faith and show the love of Christ to those around you?
pr: Dear heavenly Father, thank You for showing us, through the teaching of Jesus Christ, the difference between hypocrisy and true faith. Help us keep Your commandments not only outwardly but from deep within our hearts. Let our acts of faith always be rooted in love and sincere service, far from pretense and self-satisfaction. When temptations and trials come, give us strength, so that our lives may truly reflect our love for You. In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: “Woe to you, you blind guides, who say, ‘Whoever swears by the temple, it is nothing; but whoever swears by the gold of the temple, he is obligated.’
You blind fools! For which is greater, the gold, or the temple that sanctifies the gold?
‘Whoever swears by the altar, it is nothing; but whoever swears by the gift that is on it, he is obligated?’
You blind fools! For which is greater, the gift, or the altar that sanctifies the gift?
He therefore who swears by the altar, swears by it, and by everything on it.
He who swears by the temple, swears by it, and by him who has been living in it.
He who swears by heaven, swears by the throne of God, and by him who sits on it.
b: In this passage Jesus continues to rebuke the religious leaders of His day, especially the hypocrisy of the Pharisees. In their religious practice they valued outward form and neglected inward sincerity and righteousness. Jesus used sharp illustrations to expose their mistaken teaching about oaths and their distorted values.

Jesus pointed out that in teaching people about swearing oaths, the Pharisees made distinctions, holding that swearing by the gold of the temple or the gift on the altar was more binding than swearing simply by the temple or the altar. This teaching showed that they valued material things above the sacred places themselves. Jesus questioned this view, making clear that it is the temple that makes the gold sacred, and the altar that makes the gift sacred, not the objects themselves. He went on to stress that every oath is in fact a pledge made to God, the One who dwells in the temple and rules over all.

This teaching reveals the importance of truly understanding and respecting sacred things. Jesus calls us to recognize that every oath ultimately has to do with God, and that we should treat our words with sincerity and reverence, rather than as a means of achieving personal ends.
q: Are there inconsistencies in your daily words and actions, especially in promises and oaths? How can you take your own vows more seriously, so as to honor and respect God more sincerely?
pr: Dear heavenly Father, thank You for showing us, through the teaching of Jesus Christ, the difference between sincerity and hypocrisy. Help us keep honest and reverent hearts toward You in all our words and actions. When we face decisions and commitments in life, let us always remember that every promise we make is a promise to You. Help us live a life of complete reverence for You and trust in You. In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you tithe mint, dill, and cumin, and have left undone the weightier matters of the law: justice, mercy, and faith. But you ought to have done these, and not to have left the other undone.
You blind guides, who strain out a gnat, and swallow a camel!
“Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you clean the outside of the cup and of the platter, but within they are full of extortion and unrighteousness.
You blind Pharisee, first clean the inside of the cup and of the platter, that its outside may become clean also.
b: In this passage Jesus continues His strong criticism of the religious leaders of His day, the Pharisees and the scribes. He accused them of following small, outward requirements of the law, such as giving a tenth of their crops, including mint, dill, and cumin, while neglecting the weightier matters at its core: justice, mercy, and faithfulness. These weightier things were what they should have attended to first, yet they chose an outward form of religious practice, while inwardly they lacked these deeper values.

Jesus used vivid imagery to express His criticism, such as "straining out a gnat and swallowing a camel," to show that they were extremely careful in small matters yet failed in the crucial moral and spiritual ones. He also condemned them for cleaning only the outside of the cup and the dish while neglecting inner cleanness, a picture of how they cared about outward displays of piety but ignored purity of heart and morals.

This passage reveals a deep spiritual principle: true spiritual life is not merely keeping religious rules outwardly, but a continual pursuit, from deep within the heart, of justice, mercy, and faithfulness.
q: In your own life, could you also be like these Pharisees, paying more attention to outward religious behavior while neglecting inner transformation? How do you make sure you stay honest and active in pursuing justice, mercy, and faithfulness?
pr: Dear heavenly Father, thank You for showing us through Your Word how true spiritual life should be lived out. Help us to pursue not only the outward show of religion, but justice, mercy, and faithfulness in our hearts. Give us insight to recognize hypocrisy in our lives, and strength to become more like Christ every day. In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you are like whitened tombs, which outwardly appear beautiful, but inwardly are full of dead men’s bones, and of all uncleanness.
Even so you also outwardly appear righteous to men, but inwardly you are full of hypocrisy and iniquity.
“Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you build the tombs of the prophets, and decorate the tombs of the righteous,
and say, ‘If we had lived in the days of our fathers, we wouldn’t have been partakers with them in the blood of the prophets.’
Therefore you testify to yourselves that you are children of those who killed the prophets.
Fill up, then, the measure of your fathers.
b: In this passage Jesus continues His severe rebuke of the religious leaders of His day, especially the scribes and the Pharisees. He used an extremely vivid picture of their hypocrisy: they were like whitewashed tombs, beautiful on the outside but inside full of dead people's bones and all uncleanness. The image strongly portrays a state of outward piety and inward corruption.

Jesus pointed out that these religious leaders appeared righteous before others, but inside they were full of lawlessness and hypocrisy. He exposed this further by charging them with decorating the tombs of the prophets, which in fact disguised their hostility to the prophets' truth. Jesus revealed that while their mouths praised the prophets, they were really descendants of those who had persecuted the prophets, and their deeds only continued the evil their ancestors had done.
Through this teaching, Jesus emphasizes the importance of sincerity and inner righteousness. He challenges His hearers to examine their own hearts and motives, and not only their outward behavior.
q: In what areas of your life might you be "whitewashing the outside" while neglecting inner change? How can you live a life that is consistent both before God and before others?
pr: Dear heavenly Father, thank You for showing us, through the teaching of Jesus Christ, the difference between outward righteousness and inward hypocrisy. Help us cleanse the uncleanness within us, so that we show true righteousness to You and to others, not only in appearance but in our hearts. Give us sincere hearts to pursue spiritual purity and live out Your image. In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: You serpents, you offspring of vipers, how will you escape the judgment of Gehenna?
Therefore behold, I send to you prophets, wise men, and scribes. Some of them you will kill and crucify; and some of them you will scourge in your synagogues, and persecute from city to city;
that on you may come all the righteous blood shed on the earth, from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zachariah son of Barachiah, whom you killed between the sanctuary and the altar.
Most certainly I tell you, all these things will come upon this generation.

“Jerusalem, Jerusalem, who kills the prophets, and stones those who are sent to her! How often I would have gathered your children together, even as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you would not!
Behold, your house is left to you desolate.
For I tell you, you will not see me from now on, until you say, ‘Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord!’ ”
b: In this passage Jesus pronounces a strong rebuke on the religious leaders of His day, especially the Pharisees and the scribes. Jesus called them "serpents, offspring of vipers" and foretold that they would face severe judgment. He pointed out that the way they treated the prophets and messengers God sent was full of violence and resistance, and that these deeds would bring on them a heavy spiritual accountability.

Jesus then lamented over Jerusalem, expressing deep love and compassion for the people of the city. He used the picture of a hen gathering her chicks under her wings to describe His desire to protect and gather the people of Jerusalem, yet they refused that protection. This shows Jesus' deep grief that God's people would not receive salvation.

Jesus also declared that Jerusalem would be left desolate, foreshadowing the destruction and desolation that unbelief and rejection of God's command would bring. His farewell declaration also promised that they would not see Him again until they said, "Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord."

This passage reminds us that God's requirement of righteousness is very strict, especially for leaders and those entrusted with authority. True spiritual leadership is not merely outward law-keeping and formalism, but above all inward righteousness, mercy, and faithfulness.
q: How do you avoid becoming a hypocrite in your life? How do you practice righteousness, mercy, and faithfulness in your daily life?
pr: Dear heavenly Father, thank You for showing us, through Jesus Christ, Your love for truth and justice. Help us not only to conduct ourselves rightly outwardly, but to seek righteousness, to love mercy, and to keep faith deep within our hearts. When we face the temptations and trials of the world, give us firm faith and perseverance, so that we may follow You faithfully and show Your love in our lives. In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: Jesus went out from the temple, and was going on his way. His disciples came to him to show him the buildings of the temple.
But he answered them, “You see all of these things, don’t you? Most certainly I tell you, there will not be left here one stone on another, that will not be thrown down.”
As he sat on the Mount of Olives, the disciples came to him privately, saying, “Tell us, when will these things be? What is the sign of your coming, and of the end of the age?”
Jesus answered them, “Be careful that no one leads you astray.
For many will come in my name, saying, ‘I am the Christ,’ and will lead many astray.
b: This passage is a conversation between Jesus and His disciples about the temple in Jerusalem and the signs of the end times. When the disciples pointed out the magnificent temple buildings, Jesus prophesied that they would one day be completely destroyed, with not one stone left on another. This foretold not only the physical destruction of the temple (the Roman destruction of the temple in AD 70) but also symbolized the end of the religious forms of the Old Testament age.

When the disciples asked Jesus privately when these things would happen and what the signs of the end would be, Jesus first warned them to watch out that no one leads them astray. This is an important reminder that in the last days many will claim to be the Christ and seek to mislead many believers. Jesus stressed the importance of staying alert and discerning the truth, so as not to be deceived by false prophets and false christs.

What this passage says to us today is that we should always stay alert and hold firmly to our faith, not being led astray by the falsehood and deception of the world. In a world full of misleading information and hypocrites, discerning the truth is more important than ever.
q: In your life of faith, how do you stay alert and discern the truth? In the face of the cultural and social pressures of today, how do you make sure you are not led astray?
pr: Dear heavenly Father, thank You for teaching us through Your Word the importance of staying alert and telling true from false. Give us wisdom and a discerning heart, so that we may see through the lies of false prophets and follow Your way unwaveringly. In this changing age, help us remain loyal to You, not shaken by any deception or temptation. In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: You will hear of wars and rumors of wars. See that you aren’t troubled, for all this must happen, but the end is not yet.
For nation will rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom; and there will be famines, plagues, and earthquakes in various places.
But all these things are the beginning of birth pains.
Then they will deliver you up to oppression, and will kill you. You will be hated by all of the nations for my name’s sake.
Then many will stumble, and will deliver up one another, and will hate one another.
Many false prophets will arise, and will lead many astray.
Because iniquity will be multiplied, the love of many will grow cold.
But he who endures to the end will be saved.
This Good News of the Kingdom will be preached in the whole world for a testimony to all the nations, and then the end will come.
b: In this passage Jesus describes several events and challenges that come before the end. First He says that wars and the threat of wars are unavoidable, but He encourages His disciples not to be alarmed. This shows that these things are a necessary stage in God's plan of redemption, but they are not the end of the world.

Jesus then describes even greater turmoil: nation rising against nation, kingdom against kingdom, famines, and earthquakes. These natural and man-made disasters are only "the beginning of birth pains," a picture of the painful process of a greater plan of redemption.

In this difficult time, Christians will face persecution and even death, and the name of Christ will become an object of hatred among all peoples. This will be a severe test of faith; many will "fall away" because their faith is weak, and trust and love between people will be broken by betrayal and hatred.
The appearance of false prophets will further deceive people and lead many astray. In such circumstances, the boundaries of law and morality will blur, and the love of many will grow cold.

Yet Jesus gives a message of hope: "But he who endures to the end, the same will be saved." This stresses the importance of endurance and steadfast faith. Moreover, the spread of the gospel will not be hindered by these difficulties; instead it must reach every corner of the globe as a sign that the end is near.

What this passage says to us is that amid world upheaval and personal hardship, we need to hold on to our faith, remain faithful, and live out the truth of the gospel. It is a reminder that even in adversity our mission remains to bring the love of Christ and the message of salvation to all people.
q: In your life right now, what "rumors of wars" are making you uneasy? How do you find peace and keep hope for the future? How do you put into practice the teaching of endurance and holding on to the end in your life and ministry?
pr: Dear heavenly Father, thank You for reminding us through Your Word that even in the challenges and trials of the end times, You are still in control of all things. Give us firm faith and tireless strength, so that we may stand firm in these turbulent times and faithfully proclaim Your gospel. Help us keep love in difficult times and not be overwhelmed by the sufferings of the world. In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: “When, therefore, you see the abomination of desolation,  which was spoken of through Daniel the prophet, standing in the holy place (let the reader understand),
then let those who are in Judea flee to the mountains.
Let him who is on the housetop not go down to take out the things that are in his house.
Let him who is in the field not return back to get his clothes.
But woe to those who are with child and to nursing mothers in those days!
Pray that your flight will not be in the winter, nor on a Sabbath,
for then there will be great suffering, such as has not been from the beginning of the world until now, no, nor ever will be.
Unless those days had been shortened, no flesh would have been saved. But for the sake of the chosen ones, those days will be shortened.
b: This passage describes Jesus Christ's warning of the great tribulation at the end, quoting the prophecy of Daniel and mentioning "the abomination of desolation" standing in the holy place. It is a warning sign that severe judgment is about to come, a time of extreme hardship, especially for those in Judea.

Jesus urged those in the danger zone when the disaster comes to flee quickly and not turn back for the possessions in their homes, showing that in extreme circumstances the safety of life is far more important than material possessions. He also specifically mentioned that pregnant women and nursing mothers would face extra difficulty in this tribulation, stressing the heavy impact of disaster on the most vulnerable in society.

Jesus said that this tribulation would be unprecedented, and that if those days were not cut short, no one would survive; but for the sake of the elect they will be shortened. This highlights God's mercy and protection toward His chosen ones: even in the most extreme judgment, God steps in to protect and preserve His people.

What this passage says to us is that no matter how difficult the time, God's protection and deliverance are real. We should keep faith, prepare actively for possible future challenges, and persist in prayer, asking God to guide and help us stand firm in adversity.
q: When you face "great tribulation" moments in life, how do you find strength and comfort? What have you experienced of God's promises and protection?
pr: Dear heavenly Father, thank You for the warning and foretelling You have given us through Jesus Christ, reminding us to seek Your protection and guidance in the tribulations of the end times. Give us wisdom and strength to rely on You in hard times, and help us keep firm confidence in Your promises. Guide us step by step, so that in everything we may glorify You. In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: “Then if any man tells you, ‘Behold, here is the Christ,’ or, ‘There,’ don’t believe it.
For there will arise false christs, and false prophets, and they will show great signs and wonders, so as to lead astray, if possible, even the chosen ones.
“Behold, I have told you beforehand.
If therefore they tell you, ‘Behold, he is in the wilderness,’ don’t go out; or ‘Behold, he is in the inner rooms,’ don’t believe it.
For as the lightning flashes from the east, and is seen even to the west, so will the coming of the Son of Man be.
For wherever the carcass is, that is where the vultures  gather together.
b: In this passage Jesus warns His disciples to be on guard against the appearance of false christs and false prophets, who will use false signs and wonders to deceive, even, if possible, the elect. Jesus stressed not to believe those who say, "Look, here is the Christ," or "There he is." It is a strong reminder that the line between truth and deception can be very fine, and believers need great alertness and discernment.

Jesus used the picture of lightning flashing from the east to the west to describe how plain and universal His coming will be, showing that the return of Christ will be an event that cannot be faked or missed. His illustration stresses how visible and global His coming will be: when He returns, everyone will know, and it will not be confined to some hidden place or small circle.

The passage ends with an intriguing saying: "Wherever the carcass is, there will the vultures be gathered together." Here it symbolizes judgment and the end. Just as vultures are drawn to a carcass, the judgment of the Kingdom of Heaven and the appearing of Jesus will draw the attention of the whole world.

Through this passage God reminds us that we must stay alert, not be deceived by appearances or illusions, hold fast to the truth, and seek God's wisdom and guidance so that we can tell the true Christ from the false. It is a call to spiritual vigilance for every believer, to remain steadfast and faithful in the last days.
q: In today's age of information overload, how do you develop the ability to tell true information from false? How do you make sure you are not deceived by illusions and false teaching?
pr: Dear heavenly Father, thank You for teaching us through Your Word how to stay alert in the end times. Give us a discerning heart to recognize true and false prophets, and to stand firm on Your truth. When the world is full of confusion and misleading voices, strengthen our faith so that we can hold on to the end. In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: But immediately after the suffering of those days, the sun will be darkened, the moon will not give its light, the stars will fall from the sky, and the powers of the heavens will be shaken;
and then the sign of the Son of Man will appear in the sky. Then all the tribes of the earth will mourn, and they will see the Son of Man coming on the clouds of the sky with power and great glory.
He will send out his angels with a great sound of a trumpet, and they will gather together his chosen ones from the four winds, from one end of the sky to the other.
“Now from the fig tree learn this parable. When its branch has now become tender, and produces its leaves, you know that the summer is near.
Even so you also, when you see all these things, know that it is near, even at the doors.
b: This passage describes the signs in the heavens and the upheaval of the earth before Jesus Christ returns. These descriptions are not only literal disasters but also symbolize the end of the old world order and the beginning of a new era. Jesus said the sun and moon would be darkened and the stars would fall, showing that great change is coming. These are forerunners of the power and glory of God about to be revealed.

Jesus said, "the sign of the Son of Man will appear in the sky," meaning that the sign of His coming will be seen by all. When that moment arrives, all the tribes of the earth will mourn, because they will come face to face with ultimate truth and judgment. This scene stresses the solemnity and completeness of God's final judgment, and the glory and majesty of the Son of Man's return.

Jesus' return is not a secret or low-key event; it will be as plain as lightning. Jesus went on to use the budding of the fig tree as an illustration: when we see these signs, we can know that His coming is near, at the very doors. This illustration teaches us to watch and be prepared.

Through this passage God shows us that however the world changes, His plan and His timing are exact. He encourages us to hold on to our faith, not to be shaken by the upheavals of the world, and to actively prepare to welcome His return.
q: When you observe changes in your life or in the world, how do they affect your expectation of Jesus' return and your preparation for it? How do you stay alert and firm in faith in your daily life?
pr: Dear heavenly Father, thank You for reminding us through Your Word that however the world changes, Your promise and Your return are sure. Give us watchful hearts, so that in these last days we may hold fast to our faith and be ready to welcome Your coming. Help us live a life that accords with Your will and glorifies Your name. In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: Most certainly I tell you, this generation will not pass away, until all these things are accomplished.
Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away.
But no one knows of that day and hour, not even the angels of heaven, but my Father only.
“As the days of Noah were, so will the coming of the Son of Man be.
For as in those days which were before the flood they were eating and drinking, marrying and giving in marriage, until the day that Noah entered into the ship,
and they didn’t know until the flood came, and took them all away, so will the coming of the Son of Man be.
Then two men will be in the field: one will be taken and one will be left.
Two women will be grinding at the mill: one will be taken and one will be left.
Watch therefore, for you don’t know in what hour your Lord comes.
But know this, that if the master of the house had known in what watch of the night the thief was coming, he would have watched, and would not have allowed his house to be broken into.
Therefore also be ready, for in an hour that you don’t expect, the Son of Man will come.
b: In this passage Jesus speaks of the permanence of His words and the unpredictability of His return. First Jesus assures us that however the outer world changes, His words, God's promises and will, will never change or pass away. It is a powerful assurance that we can trust His words completely.

Jesus went on to describe His coming by comparing it to the days of Noah, stressing that people would be overtaken unawares by God's plan. These descriptions help us understand that when God's moment comes, many will be caught unprepared, just as many were swept away when the flood came.

Jesus' teaching reminds us that we must stay alert at all times, because we do not know the exact moment, not even the angels or the Son Himself know it; only the Father does. This uncertainty is not meant to cause panic but to motivate us to keep living in preparedness and obedience to God.

Through this passage God reminds us of the uncertainty of life and the certainty of the end. He encourages us to live out, in our daily lives, faith in His words and obedience to His will, always ready to welcome His return.

v: “Who then is the faithful and wise servant, whom his lord has set over his household, to give them their food in due season?
Blessed is that servant whom his lord finds doing so when he comes.
Most certainly I tell you that he will set him over all that he has.
But if that evil servant should say in his heart, ‘My lord is delaying his coming,’
and begins to beat his fellow servants, and eat and drink with the drunkards,
the lord of that servant will come in a day when he doesn’t expect it, and in an hour when he doesn’t know it,
and will cut him in pieces, and appoint his portion with the hypocrites. That is where the weeping and grinding of teeth will be.
b: In this passage Jesus uses a parable to teach us the responsibility and attitude of being His servants. Jesus describes two kinds of servants: one faithful and wise, the other lazy and wicked. The parable stresses the importance of responsible conduct and of always being prepared.

The faithful servant, because of his trust in and loyalty to his master, manages the household properly, and when the master returns he receives praise and greater responsibility. This kind of servant represents believers who, while Christ has not yet come, keep on obeying God's commands.

By contrast, the wicked servant, thinking his master was delayed, begins to beat his fellow servants and indulge in a dissolute life. His end is severe punishment by the master. This reminds us that a selfish and indulgent attitude leads to spiritual ruin and separation from God.

Through this passage God shows us that He expects us not only to serve Him faithfully but also to stay alert and be ready at all times to welcome the Lord's return. Whenever our "Master" returns, we should show the highest loyalty and devotion in carrying out the mission God has given us.
q: In your daily life, how do you remain faithful to God and actively serve others? How are you preparing to welcome the Lord's return?
pr: Dear heavenly Father, thank You for teaching us through Your Word how to be faithful and wise servants. Help us stay alert at all times and welcome Your return with holy and faithful lives. When temptations and trials come, give us strength to resist them, so that we do not go down the road of the wicked servant. In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: “Then the Kingdom of Heaven will be like ten virgins, who took their lamps, and went out to meet the bridegroom.
Five of them were foolish, and five were wise.
Those who were foolish, when they took their lamps, took no oil with them,
but the wise took oil in their vessels with their lamps.
Now while the bridegroom delayed, they all slumbered and slept.
But at midnight there was a cry, ‘Behold! The bridegroom is coming! Come out to meet him!’
Then all those virgins arose, and trimmed their lamps.
The foolish said to the wise, ‘Give us some of your oil, for our lamps are going out.’
But the wise answered, saying, ‘What if there isn’t enough for us and you? You go rather to those who sell, and buy for yourselves.’
While they went away to buy, the bridegroom came, and those who were ready went in with him to the wedding feast, and the door was shut.
Afterward the other virgins also came, saying, ‘Lord, Lord, open to us.’
But he answered, ‘Most certainly I tell you, I don’t know you.’
Watch therefore, for you don’t know the day nor the hour in which the Son of Man is coming.
b: Through the parable of the ten virgins, this passage shows us the nature of the Kingdom of Heaven and the attitude of preparedness we should have. In the parable, five virgins called wise had prepared enough oil, while the five foolish ones had not. When the bridegroom arrived, only those who were fully prepared could enter the wedding feast.

The heart of the story is to tell us to stay alert and prepared for the return of Christ. The wise virgins were always ready to welcome the bridegroom, symbolizing true believers who hold fast to their faith and do God's will. The foolish virgins, through lack of preparation, missed the chance to enter the feast, warning us not to lose our place in the Kingdom through negligence or carelessness.

Through this passage God shows us that we must always be ready to welcome the Lord's return, staying clear-headed and alert not only materially but spiritually and morally. We do not know when the Lord will return, so continual spiritual wakefulness and preparation are necessary for every believer.
q: How do you prepare to welcome the Lord's return in your daily life? Are you, like the wise virgins, always ready for the Lord's coming?
pr: Dear heavenly Father, thank You for teaching us, through the parable of the virgins, the importance of staying alert and being prepared. Help us, as we wait for the return of Your Son Jesus Christ, to be fully prepared like the wise virgins, continually growing spiritually and ready at all times to welcome You. In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: “For it is like a man, going into another country, who called his own servants, and entrusted his goods to them.
To one he gave five talents, to another two, to another one; to each according to his own ability. Then he went on his journey.
Immediately he who received the five talents went and traded with them, and made another five talents.
In the same way, he also who got the two gained another two.
But he who received the one talent went away and dug in the earth, and hid his lord’s money.
“Now after a long time the lord of those servants came, and reconciled accounts with them.
He who received the five talents came and brought another five talents, saying, ‘Lord, you delivered to me five talents. Behold, I have gained another five talents in addition to them.’
“His lord said to him, ‘Well done, good and faithful servant. You have been faithful over a few things, I will set you over many things. Enter into the joy of your lord.’
“He also who got the two talents came and said, ‘Lord, you delivered to me two talents. Behold, I have gained another two talents in addition to them.’
“His lord said to him, ‘Well done, good and faithful servant. You have been faithful over a few things, I will set you over many things. Enter into the joy of your lord.’
“He also who had received the one talent came and said, ‘Lord, I knew you that you are a hard man, reaping where you didn’t sow, and gathering where you didn’t scatter.
I was afraid, and went away and hid your talent in the earth. Behold, you have what is yours.’
“But his lord answered him, ‘You wicked and slothful servant. You knew that I reap where I didn’t sow, and gather where I didn’t scatter.
You ought therefore to have deposited my money with the bankers, and at my coming I should have received back my own with interest.
Take away therefore the talent from him, and give it to him who has the ten talents.
For to everyone who has will be given, and he will have abundance, but from him who doesn’t have, even that which he has will be taken away.
Throw out the unprofitable servant into the outer darkness, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.’
b: Through a parable about talents, this passage teaches us our responsibility for our gifts and how to use the resources God has given. In the parable, before going away, a master entrusted different amounts of money to three servants, each according to his ability. On his return he assessed them by how they had increased what they were given. Those who increased the money were praised and rewarded, while the one who did not make it grow was severely punished.

The story stresses the importance of faithfulness and responsibility, especially regarding the gifts and resources God has given us. Each person received a certain number of "talents" according to his ability, representing the gifts, time, abilities, and resources God gives. We are called to use these gifts effectively to glorify God and serve others.

Through this passage God shows us that we should not hide or waste the grace and resources given to us, but actively invest them so that they grow. This is not only material, but includes the spiritual, relationships, and personal growth.
q: How do you manage the gifts and resources God has given you? Are you looking for opportunities to multiply them, in order to glorify God and serve others?
pr: Dear heavenly Father, thank You for reminding us, through this parable of the servants and the talents, that we are responsible for all the grace and resources You have given. Help us recognize the importance of every gift and manage them with wisdom and faithfulness. On the day of Your return, let us hear You say, "Well done, good and faithful servant!" In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: “But when the Son of Man comes in his glory, and all the holy angels with him, then he will sit on the throne of his glory.
Before him all the nations will be gathered, and he will separate them one from another, as a shepherd separates the sheep from the goats.
He will set the sheep on his right hand, but the goats on the left.
Then the King will tell those on his right hand, ‘Come, blessed of my Father, inherit the Kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world;
for I was hungry, and you gave me food to eat. I was thirsty, and you gave me drink. I was a stranger, and you took me in.
I was naked, and you clothed me. I was sick, and you visited me. I was in prison, and you came to me.’
“Then the righteous will answer him, saying, ‘Lord, when did we see you hungry, and feed you; or thirsty, and give you a drink?
When did we see you as a stranger, and take you in; or naked, and clothe you?
When did we see you sick, or in prison, and come to you?’
“The King will answer them, ‘Most certainly I tell you, because you did it to one of the least of these my brothers,  you did it to me.’
Then he will say also to those on the left hand, ‘Depart from me, you cursed, into the eternal fire which is prepared for the devil and his angels;
for I was hungry, and you didn’t give me food to eat; I was thirsty, and you gave me no drink;
I was a stranger, and you didn’t take me in; naked, and you didn’t clothe me; sick, and in prison, and you didn’t visit me.’
“Then they will also answer, saying, ‘Lord, when did we see you hungry, or thirsty, or a stranger, or naked, or sick, or in prison, and didn’t help you?’
“Then he will answer them, saying, ‘Most certainly I tell you, because you didn’t do it to one of the least of these, you didn’t do it to me.’
These will go away into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life.”
b: This passage describes the Son of Man coming again in glory and separating all people into two groups, just as a shepherd separates the sheep from the goats. It is the scene of the final judgment after Christ's coming, and it stresses how much people's conduct during the great tribulation matters for their salvation. Jesus makes clear that those He commends are those who, in their lives, fed the hungry, gave drink to the thirsty, welcomed the stranger, clothed the naked, cared for the sick, and visited the prisoner. These good deeds are counted as having been done directly to Jesus Himself.

Through this passage God reminds us that a Christian's faith must be expressed in action. Every seemingly small act of kindness is direct service to Jesus. Conversely, those who ignore the needs of others will be told that they never knew Him, and will be judged for their indifference.
q: How have you done over the past week? Did you miss any opportunities to serve those in need? How do you plan to weave love and service into your everyday life from now on?
pr: Dear heavenly Father, thank You for teaching us through Your word how You will judge our deeds at the final judgment. Help us live out a genuine faith, not only claiming it with our lips but loving the people around us through real action. Give us a heart willing to serve others, so that we may be faithful servants in Your Kingdom. In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: When Jesus had finished all these words, he said to his disciples,
“You know that after two days the Passover is coming, and the Son of Man will be delivered up to be crucified.”
Then the chief priests, the scribes, and the elders of the people were gathered together in the court of the high priest, who was called Caiaphas.
They took counsel together that they might take Jesus by deceit, and kill him.
But they said, “Not during the feast, lest a riot occur among the people.”
b: This passage describes Jesus foretelling His own suffering, and the chief priests and elders of the people plotting to arrest Him. Jesus tells His disciples plainly that Passover is coming in two days and that the Son of Man will be handed over to be crucified. This was not only His foresight of His own fate but also preparation for His disciples, so that they could understand what was about to happen. Meanwhile His enemies were looking for the right moment to arrest Him secretly without stirring up the public, which shows how afraid they were of the people's reaction.

Through this passage God shows us His sovereignty and control: even in plans that seem chaotic and evil, His purpose will be fulfilled. Jesus' suffering was no accident but part of God's plan of redemption. It reminds us that no matter how great the difficulty or trial we face, God has His purpose and plan. He is able to turn bad into good and to work all things together for the good of those who love Him.
q: Think back to a difficult season in your life. How did you experience God's purpose being revealed in it? What did you learn from that experience?
pr: Dear heavenly Father, thank You for reminding us, through the story of Jesus' suffering, of Your eternal plan and the power of Your redemption. Even in seemingly impossible circumstances, Your purpose is still accomplished. Give us faith and strength to face every challenge in life, trusting that You are always in control and that You will bring about Your good will. In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: Now when Jesus was in Bethany, in the house of Simon the leper,
a woman came to him having an alabaster jar of very expensive ointment, and she poured it on his head as he sat at the table.
But when his disciples saw this, they were indignant, saying, “Why this waste?
For this ointment might have been sold for much, and given to the poor.”
However, knowing this, Jesus said to them, “Why do you trouble the woman? She has done a good work for me.
For you always have the poor with you; but you don’t always have me.
For in pouring this ointment on my body, she did it to prepare me for burial.
Most certainly I tell you, wherever this Good News is preached in the whole world, what this woman has done will also be spoken of as a memorial of her.”
b: This passage records an event at the house of Simon in Bethany, where a woman poured very expensive ointment on Jesus' head. The act stirred up the disciples' indignation: they thought it a waste, since the ointment could have been sold for a high price to help the poor. Jesus, however, defended the woman, calling what she did a good work to Him, meaning that her act carried spiritual significance, foreshadowing His coming suffering and burial.

This passage teaches us that others may judge and view our service to the Lord very differently. Through this event Jesus points out that true service is not only about meeting material needs; more important is the offering of the heart and obedience to God's will. Jesus affirmed what the woman did, emphasizing her understanding of His coming suffering and her preparation for it.
q: Think of the most recent offering you made to the Lord. What was your motive? How did that experience help you understand more deeply what true "service" means?
pr: Dear heavenly Father, thank You for showing us through the Gospel of Matthew how to view service with spiritual eyes. Help us grasp the deep meaning behind every offering, and let our lives be a beautiful testimony to You. May we always serve You and the people around us with the right attitude. In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: Then one of the twelve, who was called Judas Iscariot, went to the chief priests,
and said, “What are you willing to give me, that I should deliver him to you?” They weighed out for him thirty pieces of silver.
From that time he sought opportunity to betray him.
Now on the first day of unleavened bread, the disciples came to Jesus, saying to him, “Where do you want us to prepare for you to eat the Passover?”
He said, “Go into the city to a certain person, and tell him, ‘The Teacher says, “My time is at hand. I will keep the Passover at your house with my disciples.” ’ ”
The disciples did as Jesus commanded them, and they prepared the Passover.
Now when evening had come, he was reclining at the table with the twelve disciples.
As they were eating, he said, “Most certainly I tell you that one of you will betray me.”
They were exceedingly sorrowful, and each began to ask him, “It isn’t me, is it, Lord?”
He answered, “He who dipped his hand with me in the dish will betray me.
The Son of Man goes, even as it is written of him, but woe to that man through whom the Son of Man is betrayed! It would be better for that man if he had not been born.”
Judas, who betrayed him, answered, “It isn’t me, is it, Rabbi?” He said to him, “You said it.”
b: This passage describes Judas' betrayal of Jesus. Judas conferred with the chief priests and agreed to hand Jesus over to them for thirty pieces of silver, and from that time he looked for a good opportunity to carry out the betrayal. The passage also includes the details of Jesus and His disciples preparing for and celebrating the Passover, in which Jesus reveals that one of the disciples will betray Him, leaving all of them deeply grieved and shocked.

The heart of this passage is that Jesus knew fully what was about to happen, including Judas' betrayal and its consequences. His words, "Woe to that man through whom the Son of Man is betrayed! It would have been better for that man if he had not been born," reveal the seriousness of betraying Him and the tragedy of that soul.

Through this passage God reminds us that even in betrayal and trial, His plan continues to unfold, and that every person's choices have far-reaching effects. Jesus' openness and frankness with His disciples also teach us, when facing difficulty and unavoidable suffering, to stand firm in faith and to submit to the Father's will.
q: How do you respond when you face betrayal or are misunderstood? How does this passage encourage you to keep trusting and obeying God even in adversity?
pr: Dear heavenly Father, thank You for showing us through Your word that even in betrayal and suffering, Your sovereignty and plan stand firm. Help us learn from Jesus, so that even when betrayed we remain faithful and loving toward You. When trials and difficulties come, give us strength and courage to act according to Your will. In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: As they were eating, Jesus took bread, gave thanks for it, and broke it. He gave to the disciples, and said, “Take, eat; this is my body.”
He took the cup, gave thanks, and gave to them, saying, “All of you drink it,
for this is my blood of the new covenant, which is poured out for many for the remission of sins.
But I tell you that I will not drink of this fruit of the vine from now on, until that day when I drink it anew with you in my Father’s Kingdom.”
When they had sung a hymn, they went out to the Mount of Olives.
b: In this passage we witness Christ sharing the Last Supper with His disciples, a pivotal moment in the Christian faith and the root of the Lord's Supper. At the supper Jesus established the new covenant, using the bread to represent His body and the cup to represent His blood, which is poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins.

Jesus' words and actions remind us that He came for the redemption of humanity. This act of self-sacrifice is theologically significant, and it also sets an example for believers morally and spiritually. Jesus' sacrifice displays unconditional love and devotion, teaching us to hold fast to a noble purpose even in hardship and suffering.

Through this passage God tells us that His love and redemption are boundless, and that through Jesus' sacrifice all of us have the opportunity to be made new. The passage also sets loyalty and betrayal in sharp contrast, reminding us how important it is to choose loyalty and love in our lives.
q: Reflect on your own life: are there times when, like Jesus, you have been willing to give up yourself for the greater good? In our relationships and daily decisions, how can we better reflect Jesus' love and spirit of sacrifice?
pr: Dear heavenly Father, thank You for revealing unconditional love and redemption to us through Your Son Jesus Christ. Help us follow Jesus' example, showing our love and loyalty to You not only in words but in actions. Whatever trials or hardships we face, let us always remember Your teaching and blessing. In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: Then Jesus said to them, “All of you will be made to stumble because of me tonight, for it is written, ‘I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered.’
But after I am raised up, I will go before you into Galilee.”
But Peter answered him, “Even if all will be made to stumble because of you, I will never be made to stumble.”
Jesus said to him, “Most certainly I tell you that tonight, before the rooster crows, you will deny me three times.”
Peter said to him, “Even if I must die with you, I will not deny you.” All of the disciples also said likewise.
b: In this passage Jesus foretells that His disciples will stumble and abandon Him when He is arrested and suffers, and He specifically says that Peter will deny knowing Him three times. This prophecy reveals how human weakness and fear show themselves under extreme pressure: even the most loyal and zealous followers may fail the test.

The passage not only records Jesus' prediction of future events but also shows His deep understanding of His disciples' human frailty. His words remind us that even amid the disciples' failure, His love and forgiveness remain. Jesus knew what Peter would do, yet still chose to love and trust him, which underlines the nature of His unconditional love and the importance of forgiveness.

Through this passage God reminds us that even in our failure and weakness, His grace is sufficient. It teaches us to be compassionate toward ourselves and others, and to recognize how important it is to hold on to faith in difficult moments.
q: Think of a moment in your life when you felt you might "stumble" or give up. What helped you get back on your feet? How can you better live out the compassion and forgiveness Jesus demonstrated?
pr: Dear heavenly Father, thank You for teaching us through Jesus Christ that even in difficulty and challenge, Your love and forgiveness are always there. Give us strength and courage to remain loyal to You even when we face trials and fear. Help us learn to forgive others, just as You have forgiven us in Christ. In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: Then Jesus came with them to a place called Gethsemane, and said to his disciples, “Sit here, while I go there and pray.”
He took with him Peter and the two sons of Zebedee, and began to be sorrowful and severely troubled.
Then he said to them, “My soul is exceedingly sorrowful, even to death. Stay here, and watch with me.”
He went forward a little, fell on his face, and prayed, saying, “My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass away from me; nevertheless, not what I desire, but what you desire.”
He came to the disciples, and found them sleeping, and said to Peter, “What, couldn’t you watch with me for one hour?
Watch and pray, that you don’t enter into temptation. The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak.”
Again, a second time he went away, and prayed, saying, “My Father, if this cup can’t pass away from me unless I drink it, your desire be done.”
He came again and found them sleeping, for their eyes were heavy.
He left them again, went away, and prayed a third time, saying the same words.
Then he came to his disciples, and said to them, “Sleep on now, and take your rest. Behold, the hour is at hand, and the Son of Man is betrayed into the hands of sinners.
Arise, let’s be going. Behold, he who betrays me is at hand.”
b: This passage describes Jesus' deep struggle in the Garden of Gethsemane. Facing the suffering ahead, Jesus felt great sorrow and anguish. In prayer He expressed to the Father His wish that this cup might pass from Him, but more importantly He expressed His resolve to submit to the Father's will, showing the perfect union of Jesus' humanity and divinity.

Jesus' prayer reveals true obedience: even in extreme pain and fear, we can fully trust and submit to God's plan. This passage shows us that when facing a trial that seems unbearable, we can still choose to trust God's wisdom and goodness.

Through this passage God reminds us that whatever difficulty or challenge we face, we are called to depend on Him and to seek His will in every circumstance. This is a challenge to every believer. Let us also learn from Jesus to seek and submit to God's will in suffering, even if that will may require us to go through our own "Gethsemane."
q: Think of a "Gethsemane moment" in your life. How did you respond? When you face difficulty in the future, how can you trust and submit to God more deeply?
pr: Dear heavenly Father, thank You for the perfect example You have shown in Jesus Christ, so that we can see that even under great pressure and pain, we can choose to submit to Your will. Give us courage and strength to face every challenge in life and still trust You firmly. In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: While he was still speaking, behold, Judas, one of the twelve, came, and with him a great multitude with swords and clubs, from the chief priests and elders of the people.
Now he who betrayed him gave them a sign, saying, “Whoever I kiss, he is the one. Seize him.”
Immediately he came to Jesus, and said, “Hail, Rabbi!” and kissed him.
Jesus said to him, “Friend, why are you here?” Then they came and laid hands on Jesus, and took him.
Behold, one of those who were with Jesus stretched out his hand, and drew his sword, and struck the servant of the high priest, and struck off his ear.
Then Jesus said to him, “Put your sword back into its place, for all those who take the sword will die by the sword.
Or do you think that I couldn’t ask my Father, and he would even now send me more than twelve legions of angels?
How then would the Scriptures be fulfilled that it must be so?”
In that hour Jesus said to the multitudes, “Have you come out as against a robber with swords and clubs to seize me? I sat daily in the temple teaching, and you didn’t arrest me.
But all this has happened that the Scriptures of the prophets might be fulfilled.” Then all the disciples left him and fled.
b: This passage records the arrest of Jesus. Judas, one of Jesus' disciples, led a crowd armed with swords and clubs to Jesus and betrayed Him with a kiss, the ultimate act of betrayal. When Jesus was arrested, He reaffirmed His submission to the Father's will and pointed out that He could ask the Father to send angels to protect Him, yet chose not to, so that the Scriptures would be fulfilled.

Jesus' response reveals His deep understanding of, and submission to, God's plan. He understood that His suffering was part of the plan of redemption, and even while being betrayed and seized, He taught us how to answer violence with peace.

Through this passage God shows us that true faith is not expressed easily in comfort, but is shown in standing firm in faith and principle through adversity and trial. By His example Jesus calls us to remain faithful and obedient even when facing great personal sacrifice.
q: In your life, is there a difficulty or challenge you need to face bravely rather than avoid? How can you show trust in God and submission to Him in these situations?
pr: Dear heavenly Father, thank You for the example of Jesus Christ, who, even in the face of betrayal and suffering, submitted fully to Your will. Help us, in every challenge and trial of life, to remember Jesus' example and learn His obedience and trust. Whatever difficulty we meet, let us rely firmly on You, not on human strength. In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: Those who had taken Jesus led him away to Caiaphas the high priest, where the scribes and the elders were gathered together.
But Peter followed him from a distance, to the court of the high priest, and entered in and sat with the officers, to see the end.
Now the chief priests, the elders, and the whole council sought false testimony against Jesus, that they might put him to death;
and they found none. Even though many false witnesses came forward, they found none. But at last two false witnesses came forward,
and said, “This man said, ‘I am able to destroy the temple of God, and to build it in three days.’ ”
The high priest stood up, and said to him, “Have you no answer? What is this that these testify against you?”
But Jesus held his peace. The high priest answered him, “I adjure you by the living God, that you tell us whether you are the Christ, the Son of God.”
Jesus said to him, “You have said it. Nevertheless, I tell you, after this you will see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of Power, and coming on the clouds of the sky.”
Then the high priest tore his clothing, saying, “He has spoken blasphemy! Why do we need any more witnesses? Behold, now you have heard his blasphemy.
What do you think?” They answered, “He is worthy of death!”
Then they spat in his face and beat him with their fists, and some slapped him,
saying, “Prophesy to us, you Christ! Who hit you?”
b: This passage describes Jesus' trial before the high priest Caiaphas. It is a pivotal moment in the story of His suffering, in which Jesus faced false accusations and false witnesses. During the trial Jesus remained silent most of the time, speaking only to acknowledge that He is the Son of God when asked. This acknowledgment provoked a furious reaction from the high priest, who judged that Jesus had blasphemed, and it directly led to the decision to condemn Him to death.

Jesus' response shows His clear awareness of His mission and identity. His firmness and calm under extreme pressure display extraordinary courage and absolute trust in the Father's plan. At this moment Jesus faced not only physical violence but also immense psychological and emotional pressure.

Through this passage God reveals to us that even when we suffer injustice and hardship, we are called to hold on to faith and stand for the truth. It teaches us that even in adversity and misunderstanding, we should maintain an attitude of righteousness and honesty.
q: Think of a time when you faced injustice or misunderstanding. How did you react? How can you better follow Jesus' example in such challenges?
pr: Dear heavenly Father, thank You for the example of Jesus Christ, which teaches us how to stay firm and faithful in the face of injustice and trial. Give us strength to hold on to justice and truth even in difficulty and challenge. Help us reflect Jesus' love and mercy in our lives. In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: Now Peter was sitting outside in the court, and a maid came to him, saying, “You were also with Jesus, the Galilean!”
But he denied it before them all, saying, “I don’t know what you are talking about.”
When he had gone out onto the porch, someone else saw him, and said to those who were there, “This man also was with Jesus of Nazareth.”
